title: Meta takes on Anthropic and OpenAI with its first AI coding agent, Muse Code
teaser: Meta unveils Muse Code, an AI coding agent that tackles massive software tasks—making professional development easier by natural language description.
summary: Meta has launched Muse Code, an advanced AI coding agent that directly challenges industry leaders like OpenAI and Anthropic. Powered by Muse Spark 1.2, this beta tool enables developers to perform 'complete software engineering tasks across large repos' simply by describing their needs in natural language. Instead of writing line-by-line code, Muse Code coordinates multiple sub-agents that work in parallel within isolated virtual environments. This ensures complex projects are handled efficiently and safely. Meta aims for affordability through a 'contributor tier,' while still using the developer-provided data to continuously improve the agent's capabilities. The platform is accessible via APIs and OpenRouter.
author: Mike Wheatley
content: Meta Platforms Inc. is getting more serious in its efforts to challenge leading artificial intelligence labs Anthropic PBC and OpenAI PBC with the release of its first AI coding agent , called Muse Code. Announced in a blog post today, Muse Code is the brainchild of Meta's AI chief Alexandr Wang, who heads up the company's Superintelligence Labs unit and is tasked with leading its frontier model development. Wang joined Meta last year at a time when Meta Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg realized the company's AI efforts were falling behind those of its rivals. Muse Code, available in beta now, is able to perform "complete software engineering tasks across large repos," Zuckerberg said in a post on X. Meta's decision to develop a coding agent looks like an effort by the company to recoup some of the hundreds of billions of dollars it has been investing into AI data centers and the infrastructure that goes inside them. Coding has emerged as one of the most successful applications of generative AI, with thousands of enterprises globally now using the technology to supercharge their developer teams. For companies like Anthropic, it has become a major source of revenue, and Zuckerberg clearly believes it can be the same for Meta. Meta needs to do something. Last week, its shares tumbled following a disappointing earnings report that saw it issue a light revenue forecast and dwindling free cash flow. Like Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's Codex tools, Muse Code is meant to make it easier for developers and non-technical users to build software applications. Rather than write every line of code by hand, users can simply describe the app they need to build in their natural language, and have the assistant generate the code for them. Muse Code is powered by a newly updated version of Meta's Muse Spark model . It controls fleets of AI agents that work in concert with one another to complete complex tasks. "When a job is big enough, it fans out to separate sub-agents working in parallel in isolated worktrees," Zuckerberg explained. "Your working copy is never touched. In testing, we had it build six features for a game simultaneously with no collisions." The new version of Muse Spark was developed specifically to work with Muse Code, the company explained. Wang told CNBC in an interview that Meta is trying to differentiate Muse Code by making it more affordable than either Claude or Codex. Developers can access the tool through various pay-as-you-go tiers , including a "contributor tier" that Wang said is "more than 10-times cheaper" than any other tier. However, to access this tier, developers are required to let Meta see what they're doing with Muse Code. The idea is that Meta can use this third-party data to continuously improve Muse Code's capabilities over time. Alternatively, customers can pay a higher rate to ensure that none of their data will be retained by Meta. Muse Code is underpinned by what's known in the industry as a harness, which developers can use to manage different AI models that are customized for specific coding projects. Meta said it's making Muse Code and the Muse Spark model available through its application programming interfaces and also the OpenRouter platform that hosts many of the top performing "open-weight" models made by Chinese AI labs such as DeepSeek Ltd. and Moonshot AI. title: HPE extends validity of quoted hardware prices, possibly for months
teaser: Amid massive price hikes predicted by Gartner (DRAM +271%), HPE extends quote validity, suggesting temporary stability due to long-term deals from AI giants.
summary:
Hardware pricing remains highly dynamic amid the AI boom. HPE has extended its quoted hardware price validity until shipment to offer greater buyer certainty. This shift suggests increased cost predictability for vendors, potentially stemming from long-term deals struck by key players like SK Hynix and Micron. While these agreements help stabilize short-term prices and CXMT is expanding capacity (targeting 600,000+ wafers/month), market forecasts warn of continued extreme price inflation; Gartner predicted DRAM prices could rise 271% in 2026.
SK Hynix confirmed striking multiple long-term supply deals with major AI players to smooth volatility. The company argues that structural demand from the voracious AI sector ensures a sustained appetite for memory, despite capacity increases.
content: systems HPE extends validity of quoted hardware prices, possibly for months Suggests Big Green knows its component prices will remain steady Hewlett Packard Enterprise has changed its pricing policy and will now honour quoted hardware prices from the day of issue until the kit leaves its factories. The new policy came into effect on Wednesday. The back story to this change is the AI boom, which has seen demand for servers, memory, and storage skyrocket, and the prices for critical components rise steadily while also fluctuating from day to day. That chaotic situation saw HPE and other enterprise hardware players change policies so that the price in their quotes was only valid for 14 days. Cisco's terms were sometimes set at seven days. That's obviously difficult for buyers, who often seek a quote for hardware while they are building a business case for a new project. Big price changes could make those projects infeasible. Yet short-lived quotes also make sense for vendors, who could otherwise give buyers prices that they could only deliver at a loss. In June, HPE extended the life of its quotes from 14 to 30 days. Yesterday, the company changed the policy so that quotes that customers agree to remain valid until HPE ships products - at least for purchases of up to $1 million for its own Compute, Storage and GreenLake Flex deals. CRN was first to report the change, which The Register has verified. HPE says it gives "customers and partners greater pricing certainty and will offer greater simplicity and predictability" - and perhaps for months, because lead times for servers sometimes stretch that far into the future. The company hasn't said what has changed to allow it to revise its policies. Recent news suggests one possible factor: Memory-makers Micron and SK Hynix have struck numerous long-term deals that set long-term prices for their customers. If HPE has such deals in place, it now has greater certainty of its own costs, allowing it to extend the validity of its quotes. While longer-lived quotes are good news for buyers, they still face inflated prices for hardware. Analyst firm TrendForce recently predicted server memory prices will rise between 13 and 18 percent in calendar Q3, and ongoing tight supply. Rival firm Gartner this week found contract DRAM prices "surged" 90 percent to 95 percent quarter over quarter in the first half of 2026, while NAND flash contract prices rose between 55 and 60 percent. Gartner also predicted DRAM prices will increase 271 percent, year over year, during 2026. So while HPE will hold its prices, its quotes may still be eye-poppers if you haven't shopped for hardware lately. ®

title: Dolby Vision 2 will be available first on some 2026 Hisense TVs
teaser: Dolby Vision 2 and Samsung's rival standard (HDR10+) are set to revolutionize TVs with specialized metadata, making motion smoothing and brightness controls highly customizable for the first time.
summary:
The TV industry's pursuit of optimal picture quality continues with the rollouts of major high dynamic range (HDR) formats. Dolby Vision 2, starting on select 2026 Hisense TVs, and Samsung’s implementation of HDR10+ Advanced are competing to define future standards. Both advanced metadata systems offer enhanced features like local tone mapping, expanded brightness control, and specialized motion smoothing (Authentic Motion). These functions require new hardware (like the MediaTek Pentonic 800 SoC) and proper content encoding by platforms such as Peacock or Amazon Prime Video.
While Dolby Vision has seen rapid adoption, HDR10+ Advanced is noted for being royalty-free. The rollout signals a massive upgrade in TV capability, allowing TVs to process image information far more precisely than previous generations.
author: John.Higgins
content: After being announced last September , Dolby Vision 2 is rolling out to TVs, starting with the 2026 Hisense UX, UR9 , UR8, and U7. TCL and Philips will be adding Dolby Vision 2 support to select TVs later this year. Dolby Vision 2 is a new dynamic HDR format with a more powerful image engine and expanded metadata compared to its predecessor, Dolby Vision, which came out over a decade ago. It has two tiers: Dolby Vision 2 Max, which will be on this first group of Hisense TVs, and a standard-level Dolby Vision 2. The Max level includes a motion smoothing feature (Authentic Motion), an updated version of the ambient light sensor adjustment currently found in Dolby Vision IQ, and some pro settings for fine-tuning tone mapping. Max is for higher-end models, while the base level is intended for less expensive, mainstream TVs that don't have ambient light sensors or the motion processing necessary to drive Authentic Motion. Bidirectional tone mapping, local tone mapping, and intensity slider are all included with the base version of Dolby Vision 2, and will work on existing Dolby Vision content. Like Dolby Vision, both tiers of Dolby Vision 2 require special hardware; currently the only Dolby Vision 2 SoC is the MediaTek Pentonic 800. Older Dolby Vision TVs without the necessary hardware cannot be updated to use Dolby Vision 2, although they can still display Dolby Vision 2 content and will just ignore the extra metadata. When Dolby Vision originally came out, many movies and shows were mastered with highlights brighter than the TVs of the time could manage. So the tone mapping engine would take the picture information and fit it into the range the TVs could actually reproduce. But now that some TVs can exceed the brightness of those movie masters (which generally top out between 1,000 and 4,000 nits), Dolby Vision 2's image engine is able to work in the other direction, too, proportionally increasing the brightness of the content to fully utilize a TV's light output. Dolby Vision 2 can also use existing metadata to implement other new features, including local tone mapping and contrast adjustment, to take advantage of the increased brightness of today's TVs. While the idea of taking advantage of your TV's full brightness range is intriguing, I worry that boosting brightness beyond the level of the master could deviate from the way the creator wanted their film to be seen. Blade Runner 2049 , for instance, is overall a dark film with an average brightness level of around 200-250 nits, even though it's in the HDR format and available in Dolby Vision. That low brightness gives the film a specific mood. If I were to play that on a Hisense UR9, which can exceed 3,000 nits - or a TCL X11L that I measured at nearly 9,000 nits - would the intended presentation of the film be maintained? The premium TV world is all about most accurately displaying the director's vision - what they saw in their mind and on the mastering monitor - in our living rooms or home theaters. Once Dolby Vision 2 is readily available, I'm curious to see how drastically the brightness of a title like Blade Runner 2049 might be affected. There's also an intensity control that allows the user to adjust the punchiness of the HDR highlights on their TV depending on their viewing conditions, preferences, or contrast perception needs. It sounds similar to the HDR level settings on projectors from companies like JVC and Epson, or the HDR intensity setting in Windows for gaming. Not all Dolby Vision 2 features will be usable with existing Dolby Vision content. The most interesting, and perhaps most divisive, is Authentic Motion, which lets creatives turn on motion smoothing at a desired intensity for specific scenes or even brief moments, to minimize judder in panning shots or motion blur artifacts in a fast action scene, and then turn it off again to avoid the dreaded soap opera effect in dramatic moments. That's something that has to be added into the Dolby Vision 2 metadata during post-production; it can't be put into existing content. "That feature perhaps more than any other needs to be driven by creatively approved decisions," Jonas Klittmark, Dolby's director of business and product, told me. "We don't want to be making anything up when it comes to the motion experience." Klittmark also said while Authentic Motion supersedes the television's motion smoothing software settings, you can always override that and instead use the television's static motion smoothing settings - or turn it off completely. Making it possible for those dead set against any level of motion smoothing to not use Authentic Motion or the TVs own settings. Whether or not motion smoothing metadata is needed is up to the content creators to decide (and for forum threads to debate). But having the option there to subtly take away undesired judder or motion artifacts in specific moments, instead of a blanket setting on the TV or nothing at all, has some merit to me. According to Chris Turkstra, vice president of home devices at Dolby Laboratories, the announced Hisense TVs should be fully updated with Dolby Vision 2 by the end of September, with the vast majority complete by the end of August. But this is still just the beginning of the Dolby Vision 2 rollout. In order to fully utilize Dolby Vision 2, the content needs to be encoded with Dolby Vision 2 metadata during the post-production process. Right now, Peacock, Canal+, and iQiyi will encode with Dolby Vision 2, and other studios are working on implementing it in their post-production workflows. There's also the competing HDR10+ dynamic metadata standard that announced its HDR10+ Advanced update last fall, shortly after Dolby. It includes the same features as Dolby Vision 2 - like enhanced brightness control, local tone mapping, and support for motion smoothing metadata - and is supported by Samsung and Panasonic (two of the founders of the tech), as well as Hisense, TCL, Amazon Prime Video, and Roku. Even though HDR10+ Advanced is royalty-free (Dolby Vision requires a license), I expect Dolby Vision 2 to have wider and more immediate adoption, since companies jumped on Dolby Vision when it came out. LG and Sony have not yet announced support for Dolby Vision 2, but I expect both will begin including it on some of their 2027 models. (Samsung will never support Dolby Vision because of its investment in HDR10+). Since Dolby Vision 2 requires new TVs, it'll be a long while before it fully supplants its predecessor in the market. I think Dolby Vision 2 will be nice to have, but since we're still at the beginning of its implementation, I wouldn't put off getting a new TV just for it. title: Inevitable AI Group raises $6M to derail SaaS incumbents with more agile, AI-native software startups
teaser: AI is launching a new generation of hyper-efficient startups: IAIG raised $6M; Naïve raised $28.5M to automate business creation.
summary:
AI is fundamentally disrupting software development and business operations. Inevitable AI Group (IAIG) raised $6 million to launch numerous 'AI-native' startups, bypassing the limitations of legacy software companies by building from scratch with automation in mind. IAIG’s method allows them to challenge major SaaS players—for instance, Corebee Chat aims at Zendesk by designing platforms where AI agents handle customer support without requiring human intervention, drastically cutting costs.

Parallelly, Naïve secured $28.5 million for its infrastructure that enables developers to build fully autonomous businesses. This platform automates everything from corporate setup (like forming an LLC) to integrating essential services via API calls. Both initiatives underscore the shift towards AI-driven efficiency, enabling faster product scaling and lower operational costs compared to traditional enterprise models.
author: Mike Wheatley
content: Aleph , one of Israel's top funds, is backing a new artificial intelligence-native venture studio with $6 million in pre-seed funding so it can build and launch dozens of new software startups by the end of the year. The studio is called Inevitable AI Group , and its co-founders Nimrod Lehavi (pictured, left) and Ofer Bar-Or (right) say there's no better time than the present to take advantage of the rapidly evolving economics of software development. IAIG's goal is to identify aspiring founders and entrepreneurs with good ideas and help them to launch AI-native applications and services within a matter of weeks, leveraging the incredible advances in autonomous software development. Lehavi's and Bar-Or's theory is that because AI systems like Claude Code can quickly generate the code for almost any kind of application, smaller teams should be able to design, build, launch and then scale new software businesses much faster than was previously possible. The co-founders say they have developed a very stringent and meticulous process when it comes to selecting which entrepreneurs they're willing to back. It targets those building AI-native products in established software markets with proven demand, where clear opportunities exist for AI to increase efficiency, enhance accessibility or lower costs. Once it identifies a promising startup, it provides them with all of the tools and support they need to quickly build their products and design and execute a go-to-market strategy so they can scale in the fastest possible time. Because IAIG uses AI tools extensively throughout the entire company-building process, it says its startups can achieve feature parity with more established software vendors within weeks of them launching. By leaning so heavily on automation, its startups can get up to speed with dramatically lower operating costs than their competitors. Lehavi told SiliconANGLE that AI is transforming how software businesses are built and how they market themselves, and can help them grow much more rapidly than before. "Many of today's software companies were designed for a different technological era," he stated. "We see an opportunity to build a new generation of companies that can move faster, operate more efficiently and deliver greater value to their customers." The secret is that IAIG's startups are AI-native from the get-go, which allows them to sidestep the numerous challenges faced by legacy software companies when it comes to adopting AI. For an established firm that's encumbered with a complex architecture and an outdated operating model, it's incredibly difficult to integrate AI agents that can automate different business processes. In contrast, AI-native startups can design their entire business development and operational strategy around automation. They can therefore get by with much smaller teams, Lehavi said. Nine startups launched IAIG's modus operandi is not theoretical - it has already helped to launch nine startups since it launched itself in January, and has plans to help dozens more get off the ground before the end of the year. For instance, Corebee Chat Ltd. is an AI-native customer support software company that's taking on incumbents such as Zendesk Inc., Freshdesk Inc. and ServiceNow Inc. in a market that generates a staggering $25 billion in annual revenue. The company exemplifies IAIG's strategy. Zendesk's entire architecture, including its data model, workflow engine and pricing, assumes that humans are always in the loop, and adding AI to that requires an extensive redesign. On the other hand, Corebee's founders built the platform knowing that humans aren't needed anymore, designing it so that AI does everything. Instead of routing tickets to a human agent, Corebee's AI agents read them, retrieve the information and respond in seconds. It means a better customer experience, and because there are no humans, its pricing is much more affordable. It delivers an enterprise-grade product at much lower cost, and that is a simple recipe for success that's mirrored by every company IAIG backs. Other startups in its portfolio include Spiceform Inc. , which creates AI-powered forms that adapt dynamically to each user; VScout Ltd. , creator of an AI-native recruitment platform; Keply Ltd. , developer of an automated customer success platform; Rumore Ltd. , which sells AI-enabled reputation management software; and Mahakala , an AI-based smart scheduling application. Aleph Partner Eden Shochat said these startups all thumb their nose up at the idea of a "SaaSpocalypse." He said AI isn't killing SaaS, but it is reinventing it. "AI gives customers the ability to create tools tailored to their needs on demand," he explained. "We backed IAIG because the team understands that the winners of this transition will be those building entirely new categories of software." Holger Mueller of Constellation Research said AI is having a big impact in many parts of the enterprise, but has proven to be especially useful in code creation and business process automation. "This is what IAIG is trying to leverage as it bids to kickstart new challengers in the SaaS industry," the analyst said. "This is good for enterprises, because established SaaS vendors can definitely do with a bit more competition that will likely prompt them to improve their own offerings. But if IAIG is dreaming of supplanting those legacy players, it won't find it easy at all. It can automate the code creation side no problem, but the maintenance and support side of their business is going to be much tougher to automate. We'll see how it gets on." That said, Lehavi and Bar-Or both plenty of experience in building successful software companies, and so they should be aware of these challenges. Lehavi previously helped to found and grow a financial technology firm called SimplexCC Ltd. that was acquired by Nuvei Corp. for around $300 million in 2021. Meanwhile, Bar-Or has enjoyed a 30-year career in technology, spanning industries such as telecommunications, semiconductors, machine learning and internet infrastructure. According to Bar-Or, the most important thing when launching a software startup today is to figure out what the market actually needs and then deliver it. So long as you have a good idea, AI makes it much easier to execute. "AI is dramatically reducing the barrier to execution, so entrepreneurs can spend more time solving meaningful problems and less time navigating the complexity of software development," he said. title: Tesla and SpaceX will invest $16.8B to start building ‘Terafab’ chip factory in Texas
teaser: Tesla and SpaceX are investing $16.8B into 'Terafab,' a massive chip factory designed to power AI in robots and space data centers.
summary: Tesla and SpaceX have announced a massive $16.8 billion investment to build 'Terafab,' an advanced semiconductor chip factory in Grimes County, Texas. Spanning over 100 million square feet, this fab aims to resolve the global compute power shortage needed for future AI applications, including autonomous vehicles (Optimus robots) and space-based data centers. The facility will integrate manufacturing, packaging, and testing of sophisticated chips optimized for 'edge computing'—AI processing done locally on devices. In addition to Tesla and SpaceX, Intel is also contributing. The project promises over 3,000 local jobs, marking a significant technological and economic development for the Texas region.
author: Sean O'Kane
content: Tesla and SpaceX said Thursday that "Terafab," the advanced chip factory they are jointly developing, will be built in Grimes County, Texas, outside Houston, and that they will make an initial investment of $16.8 billion in the project. The factory will be "the largest and most valuable building on Earth by far," Elon Musk, CEO of both companies, wrote in a post on Thursday. More than 100 million square feet of manufacturing space is planned for the facility, according to SpaceX. The companies say the facility will employ at least 3,000 people from Grimes and nearby Brazos County. "The facility will be an advanced semiconductor fab that will bridge the divide between current global chip supply and the compute demand of the future," a post on SpaceX's website reads. The animus behind Terafab is that Musk's vision of the future - one where millions of robots take over human jobs, robotaxis do all the driving, and satellites become data centers for AI training and inference - requires a phenomenal amount of computing power, far more than what current production rates support. SpaceX alone has suggested in filings that it may spend as much as $119 billion on the project across a "multi-phase" construction plan - although the company didn't talk about Terafab at all on its first earnings call earlier this week. Intel has said it will contribute to the Terafab project, although it's been cagey about its exact contributions. "Terafab will be epic in both its mission and in its sheer size, designed to build new compute at an unprecedented scale and speed. A vertically integrated factory with more than 100 million square feet of manufacturing space is planned. This facility will house the manufacturing, packaging, and testing of advanced logic and memory devices," SpaceX writes on its website. "Bringing these aspects together in one location will enable fast, recursive improvements and accelerate new compute deployed. Terafab will produce chips optimized for edge computing and inference for use in hardware like Tesla's Optimus robots and self-driving Cybercabs, along with high-power chips designed for operating SpaceX's space-based data centers," the company wrote. SpaceX said in its post that it is "committing to the use of" water from the local Gibbons Creek Reservoir instead of local groundwater. The announcement followed a heavily attended county meeting on Wednesday where hundreds of residents attended and raised concerns about millions of dollars in tax breaks awarded to the project, as well as a lack of transparency. "We believe this agreement will strengthen our district, expand opportunities, and better prepare our students for their future," Anderson-Shiro Consolidated Independent School District Superintendent Dr. Sarah Borowicz said in a statement released by the Texas Governor's office. "There are defining moments in the life of a school district, and this is one of those moments. Our commitment now is to ensure that every opportunity created through this agreement is managed wisely, transparently, and always with students at the center of every decision."

title: Apple increases trade-in offers and adds new Android devices
teaser: Apple launched a new leasing program with Klarna and dramatically increased trade-in values for Macs and iPhones to manage rising hardware costs.
summary: To offset recent price hikes and boost affordability, Apple has increased trade-in offers for devices including iPhones, iPads, Macs, and even some Android models. Notably, the Mac Studio saw its trade-in value increase by $260. Furthermore, Apple launched a new 'Apple Upgrade' leasing program with Klarna, allowing customers to lease major products like the iPhone ($17.99/month) and iPad ($11.99/month) through monthly installments. This marks the discontinuation of Apple’s prior in-house financing systems. Despite the shift, Apple confirmed that users will not face functional restrictions (like 'Restricted Mode') even if they miss payments.
author: Stevie Bonifield
content: Apple bumped up its trade-in offers for iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, and certain Android phones, with some devices now worth over $100 more, 9to5Mac reports. The Mac Studio's trade-in value increased the most, going up by $260. While some devices' offers are unchanged, most got an increase of around $5 to $20, with a few seeing an increase of over $100: Additionally, Apple is now offering trade-in credit for a handful of new Android devices: While some new Android phones have been added to the list, Apple lowered its trade-in credit for a few others, including: The higher trade-in credits on most devices follow a wave of price hikes Apple announced earlier this year, with increases ranging from $30 to $4,200. Apple also launched a new "Upgrade" leasing program last month aimed at making its increasingly-pricey devices easier to afford.

title: Cyber resilience emerges as a distinct investment category as downtime costs hit $19M per hour
teaser: One hour of endpoint downtime costs an average CISO community $19 million—but only 4% feel ready for a major cyber disruption.
summary: Cyber resilience is transforming from a technical issue into a core board-level business investment. Research cited by Absolute Security showed the average cost of one hour of endpoint downtime across CISOs was an alarming $19 million, yet only 4% of practitioners surveyed felt genuinely prepared for a major outage. To truly achieve cyber resilience, organizations must move beyond basic containment drills (tabletop exercises) and rehearse their entire recovery process, including minimum viable operations and communication protocols. Cybersecurity leaders are increasingly expanding their roles to own recovery as well as prevention. Technologically, solutions like firmware-embedded persistence aim to dramatically compress recovery times from weeks to minutes by enabling remote restoration of devices regardless of their software status.
author: Thomas Godwin
content: Cyber resilience is no longer considered a mere technical concern, but a board-level business imperative and a direct investment category. In terms of recovery speed, the organizations that treat it as such will bounce back faster when disruption hits. That evolution is well underway, according to Christy Wyatt (pictured), president and chief executive officer at Absolute Security. New research published by the company at Black Hat 2026 found that the average cost of one hour of endpoint downtime across 1,000 CISOs surveyed is $19 million. However, despite growing awareness of the problem, only 4% of those same practitioners said they felt genuinely ready to recover from a major disruption. "I think the first is the cost of one hour of downtime. If we took across the - we had 1,000 CISOs participate in the survey - $19 million an hour. That's a crazy number," Wyatt said. "$19 million an hour is what the average was across that community. If we want to talk about how do we minimize downtime, we can put a dollar amount on it." Wyatt spoke with Krista Case at Black Hat USA during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. They discussed how cyber resilience is emerging as a distinct market category, why the CISO's role is expanding to encompass recovery in addition to prevention and what separates organizations that recover quickly from those that don't. (* Disclosure below.) Cyber resilience demands rehearsal, board involvement and endpoint recovery infrastructure Most organizations run tabletop exercises that stop at the point of containment. They know how to identify and remediate a threat, but they have never played the scenario all the way through to the question of how to get 5,000 downed devices back online while the business is still trying to operate. Minimum viable operations, communication protocols and device recovery workflows are the steps that get skipped, and of course, they're the ones that fail when a legitimate event takes place. "Ask yourself what would happen if 60% of your endpoint devices got wiped out tomorrow morning," Wyatt said. "Do those people know what they're supposed to do and where they're supposed to go and how they're supposed to communicate with one another?" Absolute Security's strategy for endpoint security resilience is based on a firmware-embedded technology called Persistence, which is baked into hardware from 28 PC manufacturers and covers the majority of enterprise laptops deployed throughout the past two decades. It's an anchor that allows the platform to reach a device regardless of its software state. It pulls forensics, restores network connectivity, or executes a remote, bare-metal reinstall without requiring the device to be physically returned to IT. The goal is to compress recovery from weeks to minutes, Wyatt noted. "If the answer from IT was: 'we think you clicked on ransomware, please box that laptop up and ship it back in a FedEx box,'" Wyatt said. "If we can say, actually, we'll just pull the forensics from that device, and we'll do a remote bare metal reinstall, and you'll be back up and running in 25 minutes - that's probably better." Boards that have reached cyber fluency now need to take the next step, Wyatt said, asking not just about risk posture but about what happens operationally when the lights go out. The CISO increasingly owns recovery as well as prevention, but the CFO, CIO, general counsel and board all have roles to play. After all, the research found that more than 72% of CISOs have already expanded their remit to include overseeing cyber resilience. "The right conversation at the boardroom and with the senior management team is not, have you rehearsed for a cyber event?" Wyatt said. "But have you rehearsed your overall resilience? Have you written that down, practiced it, rehearsed it?" title: China-linked LightSpy spyware caught targeting victims in 13 countries, including the US
teaser: Chinese-linked spyware 'LightSpy' has evolved into a commercial threat targeting governments and NATO nations globally.
summary: Cybersecurity researchers found that LightSpy spyware, previously linked to Chinese state actors, has transitioned into a sophisticated, commercially sold platform. This modular tool can attack numerous devices—from smartphones to servers—to steal vast amounts of sensitive data or remotely disable them. Its scope is alarming: it now targets victims in over a dozen countries globally and reportedly infects routers used by NATO member nations, providing an entry point to entire networks. The finding underscores the growing commercialization of advanced spyware beyond state-level actors.
author: Zack Whittaker
content: Security researchers say they have evidence that a Chinese-linked spyware has expanded from mainland China to now target victims in over a dozen countries, including across Europe and the United States. The previously identified spyware also has new functionality capable of stealing troves of data and remotely bricking devices. The researchers at cybersecurity firm Arctic Wolf said that the LightSpy spyware, first discovered in 2018 and previously linked to Chinese state-backed hackers, has since evolved into a commercial spyware platform operated by a single threat actor who caters to governments, enterprises, and militaries. The platform is said to feature custom branding, billing, and demos for advertising it to prospective customers. The findings underscore how the use of spyware continues to proliferate beyond governments and nation-backed hackers, and more broadly into the private industry. LightSpy is a modular spyware platform that allows whoever is controlling it to attack a multitude of different devices, including smartphones, Apple devices, Linux servers, and Windows PCs. By using exploits for each device, the spyware can steal large amounts of sensitive information from its targets, including precise location data, chat messages, screen recordings, and stored passwords. The researchers also said the code is capable of remotely wiping and destroying data on a compromised device. The researchers said that LightSpy has now been identified infecting routers, which researchers say they had not seen before. By attacking routers, the hackers can gain visibility and access to any other device on the same network. Some of the compromised routers are associated with NATO member countries, said Arctic Wolf. According to the company, LightSpy operates a network of at least 117 servers in several countries around the world. The researchers said they were able to link the latest activity to a Chinese contractor after one of the spyware's operators used the LightSpy administrator's panel to place an order with Kentucky Fried Chicken using his real name and office address.

title: AMD acquires AI chip startup Taalas to boost inference performance by etching models into silicon
teaser: AMD acquired Taalas, using etched silicon to boost inference speed 48x faster than Nvidia's GPUs.
summary: In a move challenging Nvidia's AI dominance, AMD has acquired startup Taalas. Taalas utilizes a radical approach by baking large language model weights directly into silicon to create Model-Specific Integrated Circuits (MSICs). This process significantly boosts inference speed and efficiency. The technology demonstrated extreme performance: their HC1 chip served Meta’s Llama 3.1 8B at 16,960 tokens per second, a rate reported as up to 48 times faster than Nvidia's GPUs and 8.5 times faster than Cerebras' accelerators. While this high speed comes with the constraint that users must select models carefully (as new models require re-spinning chips), AMD plans to integrate Taalas tech with its Instinct-based Helios racks, forming a full-stack, disaggregated AI platform for diverse workloads.
content: In AMD's latest bid to upset Nvidia's dominance in AI hardware, the House of Zen has acquired AI chip company Taalas, which bakes model weights directly into silicon in a process that promises to boost inference performance by an order of magnitude or more. The deal, announced at market close on Thursday, appears to be framed in much the same context as Nvidia's $20 billion licensing deal with Groq last December: make high-performance "premium" inference services prized for AI agents, like code assistants, faster and cheaper to run. AMD didn't disclose the terms of the deal, but from what we understand, this is an actual acquisition rather than an acquihire. Founded in 2023 and based in Toronto, Taalas' approach to inference is radically different from conventional GPUs or the dataflow architectures that underpin Groq LPUs or Cerebras' waferscale accelerators. A model-specific integrated circuit The startup's chips don't rely on HBM to store the model weights but rather etch them directly into the silicon. In a sense, Taalas' chips are really model-specific integrated circuits or MSICs. Perhaps more importantly, Taalas' tech isn't just conceptual. In February, the startup revealed its first test chip fabbed on TSMC's 6nm process tech, which it called the HC1. Initial benchmarks saw the chip serve Meta's Llama 3.1 8B at a blistering 16,960 tokens a second - when announced last February, that was 48x faster than Nvidia's GPUs and 8.5x faster than Cerebras' accelerators. While Llama 3.1 is ancient by today's standards, having made its debut all the way back in mid 2024, the reticle-sized chip was really intended to prove the concept. Taalas has been incredibly secretive about how its chips actually work, but we know its processors are comprised of two main regions: the mask-ROM recall fabric where model weights are etched, and the SRAM recall fabric where KV caches and fine-tuning adapters are stored. For its second-gen HC2 chip due out this summer, Taalas aims to boost parameter count to 20 billion parameters. That might not sound like much, but just like with GPUs for larger models, weights are simply distributed across multiple accelerators using pipeline parallelism. At 20 billion parameters per chip, you'd need just 50 accelerators to support a trillion-parameter model, and AMD just so happens to have a rack-scale compute platform and in-house system design team that can comfortably accommodate that. That's quite a bit more space and power efficient than Nvidia's recently unveiled LPX systems, which would need a few dozen GPUs and at least 2,000 Groq LPUs to serve the same model. From what we understand, AMD intends to pair its Instinct-based Helios racks with chips based on Taalas' tech, which implies a disaggregated architecture where compute-heavy prompt processing is done on GPUs while token generation is offloaded to Taalas-based accelerators. It's also possible that AMD could adopt a sort of tick-tock cadence in which customers initially deploy and validate models on Instinct accelerators and, once they're satisfied with them, transition to Taalas accelerators. We can only speculate at this point, but here's what AMD's SVP of AI, Vamsi Boppana, had to say about it in a canned statement: "AMD is building a full-stack AI platform that gives customers the flexibility to deploy the right compute solutions for every AI workload." You better really love that model While the tech is blazing fast, if you hadn't already figured it out, it comes with a pretty substantial downside. Once the chips are deployed you're stuck with that model. Any change bigger than something like a LoRA adapter is going to require a re-spin of the chips, which is not only expensive but time-consuming. Nearly four years into the AI boom, new models are rolling out on a nearly monthly basis. In order to benefit from Taalas' tech, AMD's customers are going to have to be really sure about their choice of models, which will be easier for some than others. However, if the startup is to be believed, the situation isn't quite as bad as it sounds. While new models will require a re-spin, it doesn't require starting over from scratch. Instead, just two layers of metal need to be changed, which is a lot cheaper and less time-consuming. With that said, we strongly suspect this tech will largely be deployed by AI model devs, their infrastructure providers, and a handful of inference providers. In an interview with our sibling site The Next Platform in February, the company suggested that etching a model's weights into silicon is 100x less expensive than training a frontier model. AMD is certainly in a position to negotiate those deals. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta are all major Instinct customers. Given the close working relationship between the model houses and the chip designer, it wouldn't be surprising to see a GPT or Claude deployed on a combination of Taalas and instinct accelerators. The tech also has implications for model development. One of the ways developers have cut down on hallucinations is by trading time for accuracy. The technique, called test-time scaling, is quite simple in practice, and involves allowing a model to "think" for longer before responding. One drawback of test-time scaling is that it consumes substantially more tokens, which makes it expensive, and means users have to wait longer for the chatbot, code assistant, or agent to respond. If AMD's Taalas buy can drive down the cost per token and boost output speeds by 10x or 20x, model devs may opt to extend the reasoning time even further. In any case, we may not have to wait long to see just how Taalas fits into AMD's broader vision. Subject to regulatory approval, the deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter. ®

title: Trevor Noah is hosting Google’s Pixel 11 launch event
teaser: Google's next Pixel launch on August 12th will be hosted by Trevor Noah, promising a blend of tech reveals and mainstream entertainment.
summary: Google is preparing for its Made by Google hardware event on August 12th at 6PM ET, featuring celebrity hosts like Trevor Noah and Alex Cooper. While the show aims for broader appeal, it will formally unveil the Pixel 11 lineup, which includes expected devices such as the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, new watches, and Pixel Buds. Leaks indicate significant upgrades but also major price increases across the board (e.g., base model starting at $899). Hardware specs suggest all phones will use the Tensor G6/Titan M3 chips, with models like the Pixel 11 starting with 256GB of storage.
author: Jay Peters
content: Google is set to host its next live Made by Google hardware launch event on August 12th, and the company says in a new video that comedian Trevor Noah will be hosting the show. The video indicates that the event will feature other celebrities and influencers as well, including Call Her Daddy host Alex Cooper (who was at the 2025 event), Indian cricketer Shubman Gill (who has starred in Pixel ads ), Japanese actress Ayami Nakajo (who has also starred in Pixel ads ), and NBA star / Google Performance Advisor Stephen Curry. (Cooper and Noah are also bringing shows to YouTube .) Jimmy Fallon hosted the show last year, an event that my colleague Victoria Song described as more like "a live taping of The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon " than a traditional tech launch event. Given the celebrity faces set to appear at this year's event, it seems that Google is once again aiming to reach a more mainstream audience. It's also airing right at the end of the ET workday: the event, which takes place in New York City, starts at 6PM ET. As for the gadgets you can expect, Google's event teaser video features brief glimpses of a new phone and smartwatch, and the company has previously shown teases of the Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro Fold . There are a bunch of leaked images and specs of the upcoming hardware floating around, too. However, if you're thinking about picking up one of Google's new gadgets, you should be prepared for a higher price tag .

title: Report: OpenAI’s upcoming AI speaker will be shaped like a donut and cost around $300
teaser: OpenAI's upcoming AI speaker will be donut-shaped, cost $300, and feature moving parts to give it an 'alive' feel.
summary: OpenAI plans to release an ambitious new smart speaker, described as a 'physical manifestation' of ChatGPT. The highly anticipated hardware gadget will take the form of a donut-shaped, portable speaker made from high-quality metal. Expected to retail for around $300, the device aims to distinguish itself from competitors like Amazon and Google by incorporating moving parts and advanced sensors to give it an 'alive' feel. Developed in partnership with Jony Ive’s design studio, LoveFrom, the battery-powered speaker will support natural voice interactions similar to ChatGPT's voice mode. While OpenAI is proceeding with development—and challenging Apple's existing lawsuit over alleged trade secrets—the device remains slated for a major reveal sometime this year, with an anticipated launch in early 2027.
author: Mike Wheatley
content: More details have emerged from Bloomberg about OpenAI Group PBC's long-awaited hardware device, which was previously described as an artificial intelligence-enabled speaker that will be a "physical manifestation" of ChatGPT. In its latest report, Bloomberg described the upcoming device as having a "ring-like" shape and said the company is looking at pricing it at around $300. OpenAI has been working on the highly secretive device for several months already, and few people had any inkling about its plans until a few weeks ago. Back then, Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman broke the news that the company was planning to launch a battery-powered portable speaker , similar to something like Amazon.com Inc.'s Echo. The report said it would be equipped with a camera and other sensors, plus "mechanical elements that can move on their own, creating a sense that it is alive and not just an object responding to commands." OpenAI is believed to be developing five different products in total, Gurman's new report today said, but it wants to begin with the speaker. The plan is to have a big reveal sometime this year ahead of its launch in early 2027. However, he added that this timeline could change, depending on how Apple Inc.'s lawsuit against OpenAI goes. The iPhone maker is suing OpenAI for allegedly using trade secrets that were stolen by its former employees who then joined the AI firm to help it develop its physical products. The reported price of OpenAI's speaker will put it in the higher-end of such products. The company seems to think it can get away with charging a higher price because of its brand name and the fact that the device will have a "premium look" due to its use of "upscale materials like high-quality metal," the report said. "The product - essentially a smart speaker without a display - will be shaped like a doughnut that's roughly the size of a hockey puck. (...) And the design should help it stand out from current smart speakers, a category dominated by Amazon.com Inc. and Alphabet Inc.'s Google," Gurman wrote. According to the report, the speaker is being designed to "work in different positions," such as being held in someone's hand or by being placed on furniture around the house. The moving parts are an attempt to make the device feel "more alive," and it will be powered by OpenAI's most advanced models to support natural, humanlike voice interactions similar to ChatGPT's newly revamped voice mode. Earlier this week, OpenAI filed a motion to dismiss Apple's lawsuit against it. The company is arguing that Apple failed to identify specific trade secrets or plausibly allege that it engaged in improper conduct. It says that Apple's complaint frames "ordinary conduct" out of context and has been filed "without adequate investigation." It's believed that former Apple design chief Jony Ive is designing the device for OpenAI. The AI firm acquired Ive's io device startup last year, adding multiple former Apple design team members to its hardware teams. Gurman noted that the portable speaker "is not something Apple has come close to launching," which supports OpenAI's claim that it has no interest in Apple's trade secrets. OpenAI is therefore arguing that it is "building something entirely new and different from anything at Apple." Apple maintains OpenAI has developed its hardware using information sourced from Apple. title: Elon Musk’s attempt at an AI Wikipedia hasn’t been updated in months
teaser: Elon Musk's AI Wikipedia alternative, Grokipedia, appears stagnant: Lawfare found zero updates across thousands of pages in the last three months.
summary: xAI's Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia championed by Elon Musk as a superior replacement for Wikipedia, appears to be stalled. Despite its growth to over 6 million articles (v0.2, Nov 2025), Lawfare reported that no entries had updated in more than three months. While the platform continues to accept suggestions, there is no evidence of recent edits or changes, leading users on Reddit and X to question if the project is 'dead.'
author: Jay Peters
content: xAI's Grokipedia, an online encyclopedia with AI-generated articles that Elon Musk once promised would be a "massive improvement" over Wikipedia, apparently hasn't been updated since April 24th, according to a report from Lawfare . "As far as we can tell, no entry has changed in more than three months," Lawfare said. Grokipedia launched in v0.1 in October 2025 with an initial batch of 885,000 articles, and is now on v0.2 (released in November 2025 ) and has more than 6,000,000 total articles, according to grokipedia.com/live . But that live page also has a section titled "Recent changes to..." with a message under it that reads "No live edits available right now." You can still suggest articles for Grokipedia to cover and edits to individual pages. But Lawfare looked at both popular and unpopular pages on Grokipedia and found that they weren't updating. "In our subsequent analysis of 34,519 pages with at least one suggested edit in our sample, containing a total of 225,496 recommended edits, we found no accepted or rejected corrections dated within the past three months," Lawfare said. xAI didn't immediately reply to a request for comment. Users on Reddit and X have wondered if Grokipedia is "dead." Lawfare also noted that Musk's last X post mentioning Grokipedia was from February .

title: How peer review keeps Black Hat’s global stage credible
teaser: In an era where vulnerabilities surface in minutes, cybersecurity events are leaning heavily on 'peer review' to maintain global credibility.
summary: As cyberattacks move at unprecedented speeds, major industry gatherings like Black Hat are prioritizing credible knowledge dissemination. The event leverages a rigorous peer-review model—managed by an independent board—to vet research papers and ensure only valuable insights reach the spotlight. This same structure is applied to the Global Startup Spotlight, which consolidates worldwide competition tracks. Industry experts emphasize that collaboration and shared solutions are critical in these rapidly changing environments, especially as many finalists build AI tools for both defense and offense.
author: Valentina Villamil
content: Cybersecurity vulnerabilities used to surface over weeks. Now they surface in minutes, as attackers move faster than defenders can respond, forcing the industry's biggest gatherings to rethink how practitioners find trustworthy answers fast. One answer many lean on is cybersecurity peer review - vetting research, startups and threat intelligence before it reaches a stage or a spotlight. Suzy Pallett (pictured), president of Black Hat, the cybersecurity industry's most established security event series, stepped into the role in Sept. 2025 after more than 20 years in global events. Pallett previously served as executive vice president for Europe and the Middle East at Money20/20, the financial technology event series. "We are seeing those vulnerabilities daily, seconds, minutes," Pallett said. "We still need to focus on the urgency and how we can come together to collaborate in critical environments to devise collective solutions." Pallett spoke with theCUBE's Krista Case at Black Hat USA , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media's livestreaming studio. They discussed cybersecurity peer review and Black Hat's new Global Startup Spotlight competition. (* Disclosure below.) A global stage built on cybersecurity peer review Black Hat received thousands of research submissions this year, but only a fraction reach the stage. An independent review board, kept separate from event organizers, evaluates every paper for authenticity and relevance before it's accepted, according to Pallett. "It's only able to get onto Black Hat stage if it's been independently reviewed by our review board," Pallett said. "Which means it's useful, it's worth sharing, and it's something critical for the industry to hear." That same peer-review model now extends to startups. Black Hat's new Global Startup Spotlight consolidates competitions once run separately across Asia, Europe, Canada and the U.S. into one worldwide track, with the winner and runner-up set to appear on theCUBE. Nearly every finalist is building AI tools for both defense and offense , Pallett said. "They have this really huge community of peers that they can lean into," Pallett said. "That's not just a moment in time when they can do that at Black Hat USA, but also throughout the year." title: Google targets AI startup Mechanize’s technology and talent in proposed $1.5B deal
teaser: Google is reportedly eyeing a $1.5 billion acquisition target—AI startup Mechanize—to boost its own coding agents against major rivals.
summary: Google is reportedly entering talks with AI coding startup Mechanize Inc. for a potential $1.5 billion deal. This proposed transaction would involve Google licensing Mechanize's technology and hiring key talent. Mechanize aims to develop advanced AI agents capable of automating virtually all knowledge worker tasks, currently focusing on specialized grading and virtual environments for AI training. Google is particularly interested in using this tech to boost its own coding agent performance against industry leaders like Anthropic and OpenAI. This deal highlights two major trends: the value placed on AI-powered coding and Big Tech's strategy of using 'acquihire' hybrid deals (instead of outright buyouts) to acquire promising talent and avoid antitrust scrutiny.
author: Mike Wheatley
content: Google LLC is reportedly in discussions with an artificial intelligence coding startup called Mechanize Inc. over a deal that would see it license some of its technology and hire a number of its most talented employees. Business Insider was the first to report the discussions , citing information from four people familiar with the conversations. Mechanize was founded last year, saying that its overriding goal is to eventually create AI systems that can automate the work done by every single knowledge worker in the world. It's currently focused on developing simulated virtual environments, evaluation benchmarks and specialized grading systems that can be used to test and train AI agents on various kinds of business tasks. Earlier this year, the startup announced it had raised $9.1 million in funding from investors including former GitHub Chief Executive Nat Friedman, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison and the podcaster Dwarkesh Patel. Its CEO Tame Bisoglu is notable for having previously co-founded the AI research outfit Epoch Artificial Intelligence Inc. Business Insider said Google is currently discussing a sum of around $1.5 billion to strike a non-exclusive licensing agreement for Mechanize's technology. As part of that deal, it would also hire some of Mechanize's experts in model evaluation and development, the sources said. It's believed that Google is interested in using Mechanize's technology to enhance the performance of its AI models, particularly when it comes to coding. That's because Google's coding agents are generally considered to be inferior to those of Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, which have seen strong enterprise adoption with Claude Code and Codex, respectively. However, Mechanize's ambitions extend beyond coding. "Our current focus is software engineering, but our long-term goal is the full automation of valuable work across the economy," it says on its rather threadbare website. The discussions between Google and Mechanize highlight two key trends in the AI industry today. The first is that coding has emerged as one of the most lucrative applications of AI models, while the second is that big technology firms are willing to pay serious sums of money to secure the most promising AI developer talent. Google has done this kind of thing before. Rather than buying AI startups outright, it structures the deals as hybrid transactions that enable it to secure their technology through licenses and poach some of their top talents. It's a useful strategy as it gets around the antitrust scrutiny that comes with full acquisitions. One of the most notable examples was Google's acquihire of Windsurf's most experienced AI engineers, and it also licensed the company's tech. Former Windsurf CEO Varun Mohan now leads the development of Google's agentic coding platform Antigravity. Two years ago, Google struck a similar deal with Character Technologies Inc. to re-hire its co-founder Noam Shazeer and obtain non-exclusive rights to its technology. Shazeer recently left Google again, however, joining OpenAI.
